J1_line_asserts_challenged_proposition.justification: The response challenges 'S can be embedded via s_alpha to alpha into the ordinal beta which is the union of all such alpha.' First-choice line 28 asserts exactly that: 'we can impose a well-ordering on $S$ by embedding it via $s_\alpha \to \alpha$ into the ordinal $\beta = \bigcup_{s_\alpha \in S} \alpha$ and using the well-ordering of $\beta$.' The active assumptions are those built up in lines 1-26: S is any set, c is a choice function on P(S)\{empty} (line 5), s_0 = c(S) (line 15), s_alpha = c(S minus the earlier s_beta) (line 24), the process stops when the remainder is empty (lines 21, 26). The singleton case is inside that scope, since line 1 imposes no restriction on S.

J2_evidence_specified.justification: 'If S is a singleton, the only index used is alpha = 0, making beta = 0, but a non-empty set cannot be embedded into the empty set.' The witness set, the index set produced by the construction, the resulting beta and the failure mode are all named; no step is left for the reader to invent.

J3_evidence_check.justification: Model-assisted judgment, supported by an exact finite computation in scripts/P03_check.py. Following only the supplied witness: with S = {x}, line 15 gives s_0 = c(S) = x; line 21's remainder S minus {s_0} is empty, so the construction stops and the set of indices used is exactly {0}. Line 28's beta is then the union over that index set of the ordinals themselves, i.e. union of {0} = 0 = the empty set (computed on von Neumann ordinals in the script). The asserted map s_alpha -> alpha sends s_0 to 0, and 0 is not an element of beta = 0, so it is not a map into beta; and no injection from a non-empty set into the empty set exists, so S is not embedded into beta and no well-ordering of S is obtained from the well-ordering of beta. The evidence therefore refutes line 28 as written under the source's own assumptions. (The script also shows the same failure for every finite |S| = n, where beta = n-1 rather than n; the reading rests on the supplied singleton witness alone.) The defect is the standard off-by-one: the union of the used indices is their supremum, not the least ordinal above them.

J4_consequence_overreach.justification: The response states no consequence beyond the falsity of the located assertion: it gives only the claim it is challenging and the singleton counterexample, and does not assert that Zermelo's well-ordering theorem or the Axiom-of-Choice argument as a whole fails.

notes: The witness turns on reading '\bigcup_{s_\alpha \in S} \alpha' literally as the union of the used ordinals (hence their supremum). A reader who charitably reads the notation as 'the least ordinal not used' would find line 28 unobjectionable; the task frame is 'false as written', which is the reading used here.
